```{r}
) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  mutate(factor = factor(factor, levels = c("Model", "Prompt", "Extended Thinking", "VoT Condition")))

ggplot(play_factor_data, aes(x = mean_val, y = level)) +
  geom_point(size = 5, color = "#2C3E50") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = ci_lower, xmax = ci_upper),
                 height = 0.2, linewidth = 1.2, color = "#2C3E50") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", mean_val)),
            hjust = -0.3, size = 5) +
  facet_wrap(~factor, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 4), breaks = seq(0, 4, 0.5)) +
  labs(x = "Mean Atoms Correct", y = NULL,
       title = "Play Mode: Marginal Effects by Factor")
```

::: notes
Play mode factor effects (using pooled data including replication runs). These factor-level aggregations are robust because they average over many games. Extended thinking is the dominant factor — its chi-squared is at least twice the runner-up. Model and augmented prompts are also significant. Augmented prompts help in play mode more than predict mode — the game is complex enough to benefit from strategic guidance. VoT conditions show mixed results, with ray trace providing some benefit.
:::

## Play: ANOVA (Atoms Correct) {.smaller .scrollable visibility="hidden"}

```{r}
#| label: play-pres-anova

# Factor setup for ANOVA
play_anova_data <- play_data |>
  mutate(
    model_name = factor(model_name, levels = order_model_names(model_name)),
    prompt_style = factor(prompt_style, levels = c("baseline", "augmented")),
    enable_thinking = factor(enable_thinking, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE)),
    config_index = factor(config_index)
  )

# Build formula dynamically based on available factor levels
play_pres_has_model <- length(unique(play_anova_data$model_name)) > 1
play_pres_has_prompt <- length(unique(play_anova_data$prompt_style)) > 1
play_pres_has_thinking <- length(unique(play_anova_data$enable_thinking)) > 1
play_pres_has_vot <- length(unique(play_anova_data$vot_condition)) > 1

play_pres_parts <- c()
if (play_pres_has_model) play_pres_parts <- c(play_pres_parts, "model_name")
if (play_pres_has_prompt) play_pres_parts <- c(play_pres_parts, "prompt_style")
if (play_pres_has_thinking) play_pres_parts <- c(play_pres_parts, "enable_thinking")

play_pres_main <- paste(play_pres_parts, collapse = " + ")

play_pres_formula <- paste0(
  "atoms_correct ~ ", play_pres_main,
  if (play_pres_has_vot) " + vot_condition" else "",
  " + mean_cells_per_ray + mean_atoms_per_ray + (1 | config_index)"
)

play_lmer <- lmer(as.formula(play_pres_formula),
                  data = play_anova_data)

# Type III ANOVA
play_anova_result <- Anova(play_lmer, type = 3)

play_anova_df <- as.data.frame(play_anova_result) |>
  rownames_to_column("Term") |>
  rename(Chi_sq = `Chisq`, df = Df, p_value = `Pr(>Chisq)`) |>
  mutate(
    Chi_sq = round(Chi_sq, 2),
    is_sig = p_value < 0.05,
    Sig = case_when(
      p_value < 0.001 ~ "***",
      p_value < 0.01  ~ "**",
      p_value < 0.05  ~ "*",
      p_value < 0.1   ~ ".",
      TRUE ~ ""
    ),
    p_value = ifelse(p_value < 0.001,
                     formatC(p_value, format = "e", digits = 2),
                     formatC(p_value, format = "f", digits = 4))
  )

play_sig_rows <- which(play_anova_df$is_sig)

gt(play_anova_df |> select(-is_sig)) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Type III ANOVA — Play Mode (Atoms Correct)",
    subtitle = md(paste0("Linear mixed-effects model<br>`", play_pres_formula, "`"))
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    Term = "Term",
    Chi_sq = md("&chi;&sup2;"),
    df = "df",
    p_value = md("*p*-value"),
    Sig = ""
  ) |>
  cols_align(align = "right", columns = c(Chi_sq, df, p_value)) |>
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = Sig) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_body(rows = play_sig_rows)
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(md("Signif: \\*\\*\\* < 0.001, \\*\\* < 0.01, \\* < 0.05, . < 0.1")) |>
  tab_options(
    table.font.size = px(20),
    heading.title.font.size = px(24),
    heading.subtitle.font.size = px(16)
  )
```

::: notes
Type III ANOVA from a main-effects linear mixed model with atoms_correct as the outcome (0–4 scale). Unlike predict mode which uses logistic regression on binary outcomes, play mode uses a linear model because the outcome is a count of correctly placed atoms. We use a main-effects model (additive, no interactions) rather than the full factorial because play mode has far fewer observations per cell than predict mode — one game per condition versus 32 rays — so the interaction model is overparameterized and absorbs real effects into non-significant interaction terms. The main-effects model tests the average effect of each factor across all levels of the other factors, which aligns with the marginal effects plot. Configuration is included as a random effect to account for difficulty variation across the 10 board configurations.
:::

## Play: Regression Coefficients (Atoms Correct) {.smaller .scrollable}

```{r}
#| label: play-pres-regression

# Extract fixed effects with confidence intervals
play_tidy_fe <- tidy(play_lmer, effects = "fixed", conf.int = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    Sig = case_when(
      p.value < 0.001 ~ "***",
      p.value < 0.01  ~ "**",
      p.value < 0.05  ~ "*",
      p.value < 0.1   ~ ".",
      TRUE ~ ""
    )
  )

play_tidy_display <- play_tidy_fe |>
  select(term, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value, conf.low, conf.high, Sig) |>
  mutate(
    across(c(estimate, std.error, statistic, conf.low, conf.high), ~round(., 3)),
    p.value = ifelse(p.value < 0.001,
                     formatC(p.value, format = "e", digits = 2),
                     formatC(p.value, format = "f", digits = 4))
  )

gt(play_tidy_display) |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Regression Coefficients — Play Mode (Atoms Correct)",
    subtitle = "Linear mixed-effects model (fixed effects)"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    term = "Term",
    estimate = md("&beta;"),
    std.error = "SE",
    statistic = md("*t*"),
    p.value = md("*p*-value"),
    conf.low = "95% CI Lower",
    conf.high = "95% CI Upper",
    Sig = ""
  ) |>
  cols_align(align = "right", columns = c(estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value, conf.low, conf.high)) |>
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = Sig) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_body(
      columns = everything(),
      rows = play_tidy_fe$p.value < 0.05
    )
  ) |>
  tab_source_note(md("&beta; = expected change in atoms correct (0–4 scale). Bold = *p* < 0.05.")) |>
  tab_options(
    table.font.size = px(20),
    heading.title.font.size = px(24),
    heading.subtitle.font.size = px(16)
  )
```

::: notes
Regression coefficients from the main-effects linear mixed model. Unlike predict mode which reports odds ratios from logistic regression, these coefficients are directly interpretable: each β represents the average change in atoms correct (on the 0–4 scale) when that factor is present versus the reference level, across all levels of the other factors. For example, a coefficient of 0.5 means that factor adds half an atom on average. The intercept represents the baseline condition — the reference levels of all factors (first model alphabetically, baseline prompt, no extended thinking, no VoT). The confidence intervals give the plausible range for each effect.

How mean_cells_per_ray and mean_atoms_per_ray are calculated: for each game, we iterate over only the rays the LLM actually fired (action == "fire" in raySequence), trace each one through trace_ray_r() to count the cells traversed (path length) or atoms affecting the ray, then average across those fired rays. These are based on the rays the model chose, not all 32 possible rays.

A note on interpreting mean_cells_per_ray and mean_atoms_per_ray: these coefficients should not be interpreted as causal effects. Causal interpretation requires that you could intervene on the variable while holding everything else fixed, but these metrics are deterministic functions of the atom configuration — you cannot change one without changing the configuration itself, which also changes the other metric and unmeasured properties like atom clustering and edge proximity. They were not randomized and only take 10 distinct values (one per configuration), so the betas capture the best linear projection onto these two features with possible confounding from correlated but unmeasured configuration properties. However, they are not confounders in the traditional sense either — they do not cause both treatment assignment and outcome. They are better understood as structural difficulty indicators: configuration-level covariates with a clear mechanistic direction (board properties → reasoning difficulty → performance). The significant coefficients tell us which structural features of the problem instance predict LLM difficulty, consistent with the hypothesis that constraint density drives reasoning errors. The honest framing is conditional association with a clear mechanistic direction, not strict causal effects.
:::

## Play: Estimated Marginal Means (Atoms Correct) {.smaller visibility="hidden"}

```{r}
#| label: play-marginal-atoms
#| fig-height: 6

# Get marginal effects for each manipulated factor
me_terms <- c()
if (play_pres_has_model) me_terms <- c(me_terms, "model_name")
if (play_pres_has_prompt) me_terms <- c(me_terms, "prompt_style")
if (play_pres_has_thinking) me_terms <- c(me_terms, "enable_thinking")
if (play_pres_has_vot) me_terms <- c(me_terms, "vot_condition")

me_atoms_list <- lapply(me_terms, function(term) {
  pred <- ggemmeans(play_lmer, terms = term)
  tibble(
    factor = term,
    level = as.character(pred$x),
    predicted = pred$predicted,
    ci_low = pred$conf.low,
    ci_high = pred$conf.high
  )
})
me_atoms <- bind_rows(me_atoms_list)

# Clean up factor labels
me_atoms <- me_atoms |>
  mutate(
    factor = case_when(
      factor == "model_name" ~ "Model",
      factor == "prompt_style" ~ "Prompt Style",
      factor == "enable_thinking" ~ "Extended Thinking",
      factor == "vot_condition" ~ "VoT Condition",
      TRUE ~ factor
    ),
    level = case_when(
      level == "TRUE" ~ "Enabled",
      level == "FALSE" ~ "Disabled",
      TRUE ~ level
    )
  )

ggplot(me_atoms, aes(x = predicted, y = level)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = ci_low, xmax = ci_high),
                  size = 0.8, linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ factor, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(y = NULL, x = "Predicted Atoms Correct",
       title = "Play Mode: Estimated Marginal Means (Atoms Correct)",
       subtitle = "Population-averaged predictions with 95% CI, marginalized over other factors")
```

::: notes
Estimated marginal means from the fitted mixed-effects model. Each panel shows the population-averaged predicted atoms correct for each level of one factor, marginalized over all levels of the other factors. Unlike the raw cell means in the factor effects plot, these estimates account for the random intercept structure and isolate each factor's contribution. The confidence intervals reflect model uncertainty. All factors — including model — were crossed in the factorial design, so the differences within each panel are causally interpretable as average treatment effects. For model, the causal claim is that choosing Opus over Haiku causes better performance, though the mechanism (scale, training data, architecture) is bundled and cannot be decomposed from this design alone.
:::

## The Performance Corridor {background-color="#f8f9fa" visibility="hidden"}

```{r}
#| label: performance-corridor
#| fig-height: 6

# Build corridor data
corridor_data <- play_data |>
  group_by(model_name) |>
  summarise(
    mean_atoms = mean(atoms_correct),
    mean_score = mean(score),
    se_atoms = sd(atoms_correct) / sqrt(n()),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(model_name = factor(as.character(model_name),
                             levels = order_model_names(as.character(model_name))))

# Create corridor visualization
ggplot() +
  # Chance zone
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -0.1, ymax = chance_EX + 0.1,
           fill = "#ffebee", alpha = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = chance_EX, label = paste0("Chance (", chance_EX, ")"),
           hjust = 0, size = 6, color = "#c62828", fontface = "bold") +
  # Optimal zone
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = 3.9, ymax = 4.1,
           fill = "#e8f5e9", alpha = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 4.0, label = "Optimal (4.0)",
           hjust = 0, size = 6, color = "#2e7d32", fontface = "bold") +
  # LLM performance
  geom_point(data = corridor_data, aes(x = model_name, y = mean_atoms, color = model_name),
             size = 6) +
  geom_errorbar(data = corridor_data,
                aes(x = model_name, ymin = mean_atoms - 1.96 * se_atoms,
                    ymax = mean_atoms + 1.96 * se_atoms, color = model_name),
                width = 0.2, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(data = corridor_data,
            aes(x = model_name, y = mean_atoms, label = sprintf("%.2f", mean_atoms)),
            vjust = -1.5, size = 5.5, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_color_manual(values = model_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 4.2), breaks = seq(0, 4, 0.5)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean Atoms Correct",
       title = "The Performance Corridor: Chance < LLM < Optimal",
       subtitle = "All models significantly above chance, but far below optimal") +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 16, angle = 30, hjust = 1)) +
  scale_x_discrete()
```

::: notes
KEY SLIDE. The performance corridor. Chance at 0.25, optimal at 4.0, and LLMs in between. The crucial observation: all models are significantly above chance — they DO extract signal from ray observations. But they're also far below optimal — there's a massive gap to perfect performance. Even the best model is closer to chance than to optimal on an absolute scale. This gap represents the diagnostic reasoning deficit.
:::

## Play: Score Leaderboard {.smaller .scrollable}

```{r}
#| label: play-score-forest
#| fig-height: 20
#| out-width: "100%"
#| out-height: "2000px"

play_score_forest <- play_data |>
  mutate(
    config_label = paste0(
      model_name, " | ",
      ifelse(prompt_style == "augmented", "Aug", "Base"), " | ",
      ifelse(as.logical(enable_thinking), "Think", "No-Think"), " | ",
      gsub("^[A-C]: ", "", as.character(vot_condition))
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(config_label, model_name) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_score = mean(score),
    se = sd(score) / sqrt(n()),
    ci_lower = mean_score - 1.96 * se,
    ci_upper = mean_score + 1.96 * se,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_score)) |>
  mutate(config_label = factor(config_label, levels = config_label))

optimal_mean_score <- if (has_optimal) mean(optimal_data$optimal_score) else NA

ggplot(play_score_forest, aes(x = mean_score, y = config_label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = chance_Escore, linetype = "dotted", color = "red", alpha = 0.7) +
  {if (has_optimal) geom_vline(xintercept = optimal_mean_score, linetype = "dashed",
                                color = "#2e7d32", alpha = 0.7)} +
  geom_point(aes(color = model_name), size = 3.5) +

            hjust = -0.3, size = 3.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = model_colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, max(play_score_forest$ci_upper, na.rm = TRUE) + 2),
    sec.axis = dup_axis(name = NULL)) +
  labs(x = "Mean Score (lower is better)", y = NULL, color = "Model",
       title = "Play Mode: Score Leaderboard (Pooled Data)",
       subtitle = paste0("Red dotted = chance (", round(chance_Escore, 1), ")",
                         if (has_optimal) paste0(". Green dashed = optimal (",
                                                 round(optimal_mean_score, 1), ")") else "")) +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9, family = "mono"),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )
```

::: notes
Score leaderboard — ranking all conditions by composite game score (lower is better). Score penalizes both incorrect atom placement (5 points per wrong atom) and ray usage (1 point per ray). This gives a more complete picture than atoms correct alone because it captures information-gathering efficiency. A model that finds all 4 atoms but fires 20 rays scores worse than one that finds 4 atoms in 10 rays. The best conditions cluster at the bottom (low score = good). Compare this ranking to the atoms correct leaderboard — some conditions shift position because they use rays more or less efficiently.
:::

## Atoms Correct by Condition: Play Mode {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: play-atoms-by-condition

# Build condition labels
play_atoms_by_condition <- play_data |>
  mutate(
    condition = paste0(
      ifelse(prompt_style == "augmented", "Aug", "Base"),
      ifelse(as.logical(enable_thinking), " +Think", ""),
      case_when(
        vot_condition == "A: Grid State" ~ " +Grid",
        vot_condition == "B: Ray Trace" ~ " +Ray",
        vot_condition == "C: Hypothesis" ~ " +Hypo",
        TRUE ~ ""
      )
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(model_name, condition) |>
  summarise(mean_atoms = mean(atoms_correct), .groups = "drop")

# Order condition legend by mean atoms correct (highest to lowest = best to worst)
condition_order_atoms <- play_atoms_by_condition |>
  group_by(condition) |>
  summarise(sum_atoms = sum(mean_atoms)) |>
  arrange(desc(sum_atoms)) |>
  pull(condition)
play_atoms_by_condition$condition <- factor(play_atoms_by_condition$condition,
                                            levels = condition_order_atoms)

# Order models by size
play_atoms_by_condition$model_name <- factor(
  play_atoms_by_condition$model_name,
  levels = order_model_names(unique(play_atoms_by_condition$model_name)))

n_cond_atoms <- n_distinct(play_atoms_by_condition$condition)
atoms_cond_colors <- colorRampPalette(RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(8, "Dark2"))(n_cond_atoms)

p <- ggplot(play_atoms_by_condition, aes(x = model_name, y = mean_atoms,
                                 color = condition, group = condition,
                                 text = paste0("Condition: ", condition,
                                               "\nModel: ", model_name,
                                               "\nMean Atoms Correct: ",
                                               round(mean_atoms, 2)))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = atoms_cond_colors) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean Atoms Correct", color = "Condition",
       title = "Play Mode: Atoms Correct by Experimental Condition",
       subtitle = "Each line = one prompt × thinking × VoT combination") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1),
        legend.position = "right")

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") |>
  layout(hoverlabel = list(bgcolor = "white"),
         margin = list(r = 150)) |>
  htmlwidgets::onRender("
    function(el) {
      var highlighted = null;
      el.on('plotly_legendclick', function(d) {
        var clickedGroup = el.data[d.curveNumber].legendgroup;
        if (highlighted === clickedGroup) {
          Plotly.restyle(el, {opacity: 1});
          highlighted = null;
        } else {
          for (var i = 0; i < el.data.length; i++) {
            var op = (el.data[i].legendgroup === clickedGroup) ? 1 : 0.2;
            Plotly.restyle(el, {opacity: op}, [i]);
          }
          highlighted = clickedGroup;
        }
        return false;
      });
      el.on('plotly_legenddoubleclick', function() {
        Plotly.restyle(el, {opacity: 1});
        highlighted = null;
        return false;
      });
    }
  ")
```

::: notes
Play mode atoms correct by experimental condition, with models ordered by size. Lines higher on the chart mean more atoms correctly placed. Conditions that maintain consistent ranking across models suggest additive effects; crossings indicate interaction effects. Unlike predict mode error counts, this uses the mean atoms correct (0–4 scale) averaged across configurations.
:::

## LLM vs Optimal: Rays Used

```{r}
#| label: optimal-rays
#| eval: !expr has_optimal

# Best condition identification
best_condition_lookup <- play_data |>
  mutate(condition = paste0(model_name, " | ",
    ifelse(prompt_style == "augmented", "Aug", "Base"), " | ",
    ifelse(as.logical(as.character(enable_thinking)), "Think", "No-Think"), " | ",
    case_when(vot_grid_state ~ "A: Grid State", vot_ray_trace ~ "B: Ray Trace",
              vot_hypothesis ~ "C: Hypothesis", TRUE ~ "None"))) |>
  group_by(condition, model_name) |>
  summarise(score_mean = mean(score), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(score_mean) |> slice(1)
best_short_label <- paste0("Best (", best_condition_lookup$model_name, ")")

best_config_agg <- play_data |>
  mutate(condition = paste0(model_name, " | ",
    ifelse(prompt_style == "augmented", "Aug", "Base"), " | ",
    ifelse(as.logical(as.character(enable_thinking)), "Think", "No-Think"), " | ",
    case_when(vot_grid_state ~ "A: Grid State", vot_ray_trace ~ "B: Ray Trace",
              vot_hypothesis ~ "C: Hypothesis", TRUE ~ "None"))) |>
  filter(condition == best_condition_lookup$condition) |>
  group_by(config_index) |>
  summarise(best_rays_mean = mean(rays_used), best_score_mean = mean(score), .groups = "drop")

play_config_agg <- play_data |>
  group_by(config_index) |>
  summarise(llm_rays_mean = mean(rays_used), llm_score_mean = mean(score), .groups = "drop")

comparison <- inner_join(play_config_agg, optimal_data, by = "config_index") |>
  left_join(best_config_agg, by = "config_index")

rays_long <- comparison |>
  select(config_index, optimal_rays, best_rays_mean, llm_rays_mean) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(optimal_rays, best_rays_mean, llm_rays_mean),
               names_to = "agent", values_to = "rays") |>
  mutate(agent = case_when(
    agent == "optimal_rays" ~ "Optimal Solver",
    agent == "best_rays_mean" ~ best_short_label,
    TRUE ~ "LLM (Mean)")) |>
  mutate(agent = factor(agent, levels = c("Optimal Solver", best_short_label, "LLM (Mean)")))

ggplot(rays_long, aes(x = config_index, y = rays, color = agent, group = agent)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = setNames(c("#2196F3", "#4CAF50", "#FF9800"),
    c("Optimal Solver", best_short_label, "LLM (Mean)"))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:9) +
  labs(x = "Configuration", y = "Rays Used", color = NULL,
       title = "Rays Used: Optimal vs Best Condition vs LLM Mean",
       subtitle = "LLMs consistently use more rays — poor test selection efficiency",
       caption = "Best condition selected by lowest mean score")
```

::: notes
Configuration-by-configuration comparison of rays used. Blue is the optimal solver, green is the best LLM condition, orange is the overall LLM mean. LLMs consistently use 2-3× as many rays as optimal. This is the test selection problem — LLMs are not choosing informative rays. They fire redundant rays that don't narrow the candidate space efficiently. Direct analog to ordering redundant lab tests.
:::

## Cross-Mode Comparison {visibility="hidden"}

```{r}
#| label: cross-mode

predict_model_agg <- predict_data |>
  group_by(model_name) |>
  summarise(predict_accuracy = mean(correct),
            predict_se = sqrt(predict_accuracy * (1 - predict_accuracy) / n()),
            .groups = "drop")

play_model_agg <- play_data |>
  group_by(model_name) |>
  summarise(play_atoms_pct = mean(atoms_correct) / 4,
            play_atoms_se = sd(atoms_correct) / (4 * sqrt(n())),
            .groups = "drop")

model_comparison <- inner_join(predict_model_agg, play_model_agg, by = "model_name") |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(predict_accuracy, play_atoms_pct),
               names_to = "mode", values_to = "performance") |>
  mutate(
    se = ifelse(mode == "predict_accuracy", predict_se, play_atoms_se),
    mode = ifelse(mode == "predict_accuracy", "Predict (Accuracy)", "Play (Atoms Correct %)")
  )

ggplot(model_comparison, aes(x = model_name, y = performance, fill = mode)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = performance - 1.96 * se, ymax = performance + 1.96 * se),
                position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Predict (Accuracy)" = "#3498db", "Play (Atoms Correct %)" = "#e74c3c")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Performance", fill = "Mode",
       title = "Forward vs Inverse Reasoning by Model",
       subtitle = "All models show a gap: forward reasoning (predict) outperforms inverse reasoning (play)") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

::: notes
Head-to-head comparison. Blue is predict mode — forward reasoning. Red is play mode — full diagnostic loop. The gap is consistent across all models: forward reasoning is easier than inverse reasoning. This makes theoretical sense — prediction is deductive, diagnosis is abductive. But the gap also reveals that the inferential machinery (hypothesis generation, test selection, constraint tracking) adds substantial difficulty beyond just spatial reasoning.
:::

## The Test Selection Problem

```{r}
#| label: ray-rank-histogram
#| eval: !expr has_det_play
#| fig-height: 5.5

non_excess_rays <- det_rays |> filter(!is_excess)

# Use percentile rank if available (corrects for shrinking action space),
# otherwise fall back to raw rank.
if ("llm_rank_percentile" %in% names(non_excess_rays) &&
    any(!is.na(non_excess_rays$llm_rank_percentile))) {
  ggplot(non_excess_rays |> filter(!is.na(llm_rank_percentile)),
         aes(x = llm_rank_percentile)) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, fill = "#2ecc71", color = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1) +
    facet_wrap(~model_name, scales = "free_y") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
    labs(x = "Ray Rank Percentile (among remaining unfired rays)",
         y = "Count",
         title = "Distribution of Normalized Ray Selection Rank by Model",
         subtitle = "0% = optimal; normalized for shrinking action space as rays are used") +
    theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 14))
} else {
  ggplot(non_excess_rays, aes(x = llm_rank)) +
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#3498db", color = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1) +
    facet_wrap(~model_name, scales = "free_y") +
    labs(x = "LLM Ray Rank (competition ranking, among remaining unfired rays)",
         y = "Count",
         title = "Distribution of Ray Selection Rank by Model",
         subtitle = "Rank 1 = optimal (ties share rank). Dashed red = optimal.") +
    theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 14))
}
```

::: fragment
**Clinical analog**: Choosing which diagnostic test to order next. Models rarely pick the most informative option — analogous to ordering a comprehensive metabolic panel when a single targeted test would be more informative.
:::

::: notes
The test selection problem visualized. For each ray the model fires, we compute its percentile rank among all remaining unfired rays by information content. 0% is the information-theoretically optimal choice. The percentile normalization corrects for the shrinking action space — as rays are used, fewer remain, so raw ranks become artificially compressed toward lower values. The distributions show that models rarely pick the optimal ray. This is the clinical analog of choosing which test to order next. An optimal diagnostician picks the test that rules out the most conditions. LLMs pick tests somewhat informatively but far from optimal. In clinical practice, this manifests as redundant testing and delayed diagnosis.
:::

## Error Analysis: Deterministic

```{r}
#| label: play-errors-det
#| eval: !expr has_det_play
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-width: 12
#| out-width: "100%"

det_ray_summary <- det_games |>
  group_by(model_name) |>
  summarise(
    pct_optimal = round(sum(n_optimal_rays) / sum(total_rays_fired) * 100, 1),
    mean_rank = round(mean(mean_ray_rank, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    mean_excess = round(mean(excess_rays, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

det_summary_long <- det_ray_summary |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(pct_optimal, mean_rank, mean_excess),
               names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(metric = case_when(
    metric == "pct_optimal" ~ "% Optimal Rays",
    metric == "mean_rank" ~ "Mean Ray Rank",
    metric == "mean_excess" ~ "Mean Excess Rays"
  ))

ggplot(det_summary_long, aes(x = model_name, y = value, fill = model_name)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(value, 1)), vjust = -0.3, size = 4.5) +
  facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = model_colors) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "Deterministic Analysis",
       subtitle = "Ray quality, ranking, and excess") +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

::: notes
Deterministic analysis of play mode. We replay each model's ray sequences through the full candidate space to measure decision quality objectively. Models pick optimal rays only a fraction of the time, with typical ray ranks around 5-10 out of 32 possible rays. They also fire excess rays after the solution is already determinable — they don't know when to stop.
:::

```{r}

play_spatial_by_model <- play_errors |>

  ungroup()

ggplot(play_spatial_by_model,
       aes(x = model_name, y = pct, fill = error_domain)) +

```

::: notes
LLM-as-judge classification of play mode errors into spatial versus non-spatial failures. Non-spatial errors — experiment design, constraint tracking, belief updating — dominate across all models. Spatial reasoning is not the bottleneck; the inferential machinery is.
:::

## Replication

- 80 experimental conditions, each tested on only **n = 10 game boards**
- Top two configurations by atoms correct:
  1. **Opus 4.6** — Augmented, Thinking, VoT Ray Trace → **3.10 mean**
  2. **Sonnet 4.6** — Augmented, Thinking, VoT Ray Trace → **3.00 mean**
- With n = 10, confidence intervals are wide — are these truly the best, or just lucky draws?
- **Winner's curse**: selecting the top performers from 80 noisy estimates guarantees upward bias
- Replication: ran both configs **8 more times** on the same 10 boards (n = 10 → 90 per config)
- Does the observed ranking reflect real performance or sampling noise?

::: notes
Before showing the replication data, it's worth explaining why we ran it. With 80 experimental conditions each tested on only 10 game boards, our estimates of mean atoms correct carry substantial uncertainty. The top two configs — both using augmented prompts, extended thinking, and VoT ray trace — scored 3.10 and 3.00 out of 4. But with n=10, a single lucky or unlucky board swings the mean by 0.4. When you pick the best from 80 noisy estimates, you're selecting on noise as much as signal. This is the classic winner's curse problem from auction theory. So we ran both configurations 8 more times on the same 10 game boards, bringing each from n=10 to n=90.
:::

## Replication: Atoms Correct With More Data {.smaller .scrollable}

```{r}
#| label: play-replication-slide
#| fig-height: 20
#| out-width: "100%"
#| out-height: "2000px"

if (n_replication_runs > 0) {
  # Build comparison: original vs pooled for replicated configs, original-only for others
  forest_original <- play_data_original |>
    mutate(
      config_label = paste0(
        model_name, " | ",
        ifelse(prompt_style == "augmented", "Aug", "Base"), " | ",
        ifelse(as.logical(enable_thinking), "Think", "No-Think"), " | ",
        gsub("^[A-C]: ", "", as.character(vot_condition))
      )
    ) |>
    group_by(config_label, model_name, prompt_style, enable_thinking,
             vot_grid_state, vot_ray_trace, vot_hypothesis) |>
    summarise(
      n = n(), mean_correct = mean(atoms_correct),
      se = sd(atoms_correct) / sqrt(n()),
      ci_lower = mean_correct - 1.96 * se,
      ci_upper = mean_correct + 1.96 * se,
      .groups = "drop"
    )

  forest_pooled <- play_data |>
    mutate(
      config_label = paste0(
        model_name, " | ",
        ifelse(prompt_style == "augmented", "Aug", "Base"), " | ",
        ifelse(as.logical(enable_thinking), "Think", "No-Think"), " | ",
        gsub("^[A-C]: ", "", as.character(vot_condition))
      )
    ) |>
    group_by(config_label, model_name, prompt_style, enable_thinking,
             vot_grid_state, vot_ray_trace, vot_hypothesis) |>
    summarise(
      n = n(), mean_correct = mean(atoms_correct),
      se = sd(atoms_correct) / sqrt(n()),
      ci_lower = mean_correct - 1.96 * se,
      ci_upper = mean_correct + 1.96 * se,
      .groups = "drop"
    )

  # Identify replicated configs
  forest_pooled <- forest_pooled |>
    mutate(
      replicated = pmap_lgl(list(model_name, prompt_style, enable_thinking,
                                  vot_grid_state, vot_ray_trace, vot_hypothesis),
        function(mn, ps, et, vgs, vrt, vh) {
          any(replicated_conditions$model_name == mn &
              replicated_conditions$prompt_style == ps &
              replicated_conditions$enable_thinking == et &
              replicated_conditions$vot_grid_state == vgs &
              replicated_conditions$vot_ray_trace == vrt &
              replicated_conditions$vot_hypothesis == vh)
        }),
      label_display = ifelse(replicated,
                             paste0(config_label, " (n=", n, ")"),
                             config_label)
    ) |>
    arrange(mean_correct) |>
    mutate(label_display = factor(label_display, levels = label_display))

  # Show original means as hollow points for replicated configs
  original_replicated <- forest_original |>
    semi_join(replicated_conditions,
              by = c("model_name", "prompt_style", "enable_thinking",
                     "vot_grid_state", "vot_ray_trace", "vot_hypothesis")) |>
    left_join(forest_pooled |> select(config_label, label_display),
              by = "config_label")

  ggplot(forest_pooled, aes(x = mean_correct, y = label_display)) +
    geom_point(aes(color = model_name, shape = replicated), size = 3.5) +
    geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = ci_lower, xmax = ci_upper, color = model_name),
                   height = 0.3, linewidth = 0.9) +
    # Show original means as hollow circles for replicated configs
    geom_point(data = original_replicated,
               aes(x = mean_correct, y = label_display),
               shape = 1, size = 4, color = "gray40", stroke = 1.2) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0.25, linetype = "dotted", color = "red", alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50", alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", mean_correct)),
              hjust = -0.3, size = 3.5) +
    scale_color_manual(values = model_colors) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c("FALSE" = 16, "TRUE" = 17), guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 4.2), breaks = seq(0, 4, 0.5),
                       sec.axis = dup_axis(name = NULL)) +
    labs(x = "Mean Atoms Correct (out of 4)", y = NULL, color = "Model",
         title = "Play Mode: Atoms Correct — Pooled Results (replication shifts rankings)",
         subtitle = "Filled = pooled mean. Hollow circle = original n=10 mean for replicated configs.") +
    theme(
      axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9, family = "mono"),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
    )
}
```

::: notes
When we replicated the top two configurations 4 additional times on the same game boards, both regressed toward the mean. The hollow circles show where they originally ranked; the filled triangles show the pooled result. The original n=10 was a lucky draw — both top configs sat at the upper tail of their actual performance distributions. This is classic winner's curse: select the best from 80 noisy estimates, and you've selected noise along with signal.
:::

## Performance Variance as a Finding {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: play-variance-slide
#| fig-height: 7

if (n_replication_runs > 0) {
  heatmap_data <- play_data |>
    semi_join(replicated_conditions,
              by = c("model_name", "prompt_style", "enable_thinking",
                     "vot_grid_state", "vot_ray_trace", "vot_hypothesis")) |>
    mutate(run_label = ifelse(source == "original", "Original",
                              paste0("Run ", as.integer(factor(run_id)))))

  ggplot(heatmap_data,
         aes(x = run_label, y = factor(config_index), fill = atoms_correct)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_text(aes(label = atoms_correct), size = 5, fontface = "bold") +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#c62828", mid = "#fff176", high = "#2e7d32",
                         midpoint = 2, limits = c(0, 4),
                         name = "Atoms\nCorrect") +
    facet_wrap(~model_name, ncol = 2) +
    labs(
      title = "Per-Configuration Reliability Across Runs",
      subtitle = "Same boards, same config — performance swings wildly on some boards, not others",
      x = NULL, y = "Game Board"
    ) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 11),
          axis.text.y = element_text(size = 12),
          strip.text = element_text(size = 13))
}
```

::: notes
This heatmap is the key finding. Each row is a game board, each column is a run. Green means all 4 atoms found, red means failure. Look at boards 2 and 6 — reliably solved every single time, both models. These are configurations where the model has stable access to the reasoning needed. But other boards (like 4 and 5) swing between 0 and 4 across runs. This is not consistent partial competence — it's stochastic access to a reasoning strategy. The model either finds the right approach or doesn't, with little middle ground. This bimodal pattern is itself diagnostic of how LLMs reason about constraint satisfaction.
:::

## Scaling Effects {visibility="hidden"}

```{r}
#| label: scaling

# Model-level summary across both modes
scaling_data <- bind_rows(
  predict_data |>
    group_by(model_name) |>
    summarise(value = mean(correct), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(metric = "Predict Accuracy"),
  play_data |>
    group_by(model_name) |>
    summarise(value = mean(atoms_correct) / 4, .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(metric = "Play Atoms Correct (%)")
) |>
  mutate(
    model_name = factor(as.character(model_name),
                        levels = order_model_names(as.character(model_name))),
    metric = factor(metric, levels = c("Predict Accuracy", "Play Atoms Correct (%)"))
  )

ggplot(scaling_data, aes(x = model_name, y = value, fill = metric)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(value * 100, 1), "%")),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), vjust = -0.3, size = 5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Predict Accuracy" = "#3498db",
                                "Play Atoms Correct (%)" = "#e74c3c")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Performance", fill = "Mode",
       title = "Scaling: Haiku → Sonnet → Opus",
       subtitle = "Larger models improve in both modes, but the predict-play gap persists") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

::: notes
Scaling from Haiku to Opus. Both modes improve with model size, but the gap between predict and play performance persists. Larger models are better at spatial reasoning AND at the full diagnostic loop, but they don't close the gap between the two. This suggests the diagnostic reasoning deficit isn't just a matter of scale — it's a qualitative limitation in how these models integrate component processes.
:::

## Factor Summary

```{r}
#| label: factor-summary-table

# ── Helpers ──
fs_get_p <- function(res, term) {
  df <- as.data.frame(res) |> rownames_to_column("term")
  p <- df$`Pr(>Chisq)`[df$term == term]
  if (length(p) == 0) NA_real_ else p[1]
}

fs_get_chi <- function(res, term) {
  df <- as.data.frame(res) |> rownames_to_column("term")
  v <- df$Chisq[df$term == term]
  if (length(v) == 0) NA_real_ else v[1]
}

fs_arrow <- function(p_val, effect_size, is_dominant = FALSE) {
  if (is.na(p_val) || p_val >= 0.10) return("\u2014")
  if (p_val >= 0.05) {
    if (effect_size > 0) return("\u2014 / \u2191")
    if (effect_size < 0) return("\u2014 / \u2193")
    return("\u2014")
  }
  if (is_dominant && effect_size > 0) return("\u2191\u2191")
  if (effect_size > 0) return("\u2191")
  if (effect_size < 0) return("\u2193")
  "\u2014"
}

# Dominant = highest chi-sq among significant terms, and >= 2x runner-up
fs_find_dominant <- function(ps, chis) {
  sig <- names(ps)[!is.na(ps) & ps < 0.05]
  sig_chis <- chis[sig]; sig_chis <- sig_chis[!is.na(sig_chis)]
  if (length(sig_chis) < 2) return(if (length(sig_chis) == 1) names(sig_chis) else NULL)
  s <- sort(sig_chis, decreasing = TRUE)
  if (s[1] >= 2 * s[2]) names(which.max(sig_chis)) else NULL
}

fs_safe_diff <- function(vals, labels, hi, lo) {
  h <- vals[labels == hi]; l <- vals[labels == lo]
  if (length(h) > 0 && length(l) > 0) h[1] - l[1] else 0
}

fs_is_dom <- function(dom, name) !is.null(dom) && dom == name

# ── Predict mode ──
pred_p <- c(model = fs_get_p(anova_result, "model_name"),
            prompt = fs_get_p(anova_result, "prompt_style"),
            thinking = fs_get_p(anova_result, "enable_thinking"),
            vot = fs_get_p(anova_result, "vot_ray_trace"))
pred_chi <- c(model = fs_get_chi(anova_result, "model_name"),
              prompt = fs_get_chi(anova_result, "prompt_style"),
              thinking = fs_get_chi(anova_result, "enable_thinking"),
              vot = fs_get_chi(anova_result, "vot_ray_trace"))
pred_dom <- fs_find_dominant(pred_p, pred_chi)

pred_model_eff <- diff(range(factor_data$accuracy[factor_data$factor == "Model"]))
fd_pr <- factor_data |> filter(factor == "Prompt")
pred_prompt_eff <- fs_safe_diff(fd_pr$accuracy, fd_pr$level, "augmented", "baseline")
fd_th <- factor_data |> filter(factor == "Extended Thinking")
pred_think_eff <- fs_safe_diff(fd_th$accuracy, fd_th$level, "Enabled", "Disabled")
fd_vt <- factor_data |> filter(factor == "VoT Ray Trace")
pred_vot_eff <- fs_safe_diff(fd_vt$accuracy, fd_vt$level, "Enabled", "Disabled")

# ── Play mode ──
play_p <- c(model = fs_get_p(play_anova_result, "model_name"),
            prompt = fs_get_p(play_anova_result, "prompt_style"),
            thinking = fs_get_p(play_anova_result, "enable_thinking"),
            vot = fs_get_p(play_anova_result, "vot_condition"))
play_chi <- c(model = fs_get_chi(play_anova_result, "model_name"),
              prompt = fs_get_chi(play_anova_result, "prompt_style"),
              thinking = fs_get_chi(play_anova_result, "enable_thinking"),
              vot = fs_get_chi(play_anova_result, "vot_condition"))
play_dom <- fs_find_dominant(play_p, play_chi)

play_model_eff <- diff(range(play_factor_data$mean_val[play_factor_data$factor == "Model"]))
pfd_pr <- play_factor_data |> filter(factor == "Prompt")
play_prompt_eff <- fs_safe_diff(pfd_pr$mean_val, pfd_pr$level, "augmented", "baseline")
pfd_th <- play_factor_data |> filter(factor == "Extended Thinking")
play_think_eff <- fs_safe_diff(pfd_th$mean_val, pfd_th$level, "Enabled", "Disabled")

# VoT individual effects in play
pfd_vot <- play_factor_data |> filter(factor == "VoT Condition")
vot_none_val <- pfd_vot$mean_val[pfd_vot$level == "None"]
if (length(vot_none_val) == 0) vot_none_val <- NA_real_

fs_vot_eff <- function(pat) {
  if (is.na(vot_none_val)) return(0)
  v <- pfd_vot$mean_val[grepl(pat, pfd_vot$level)]
  if (length(v) == 0) 0 else v[1] - vot_none_val
}

fs_vot_arrow <- function(p_overall, eff) {
  if (is.na(p_overall) || p_overall >= 0.10) return("\u2014")
  if (p_overall >= 0.05) {
    if (eff > 0.1) return("\u2014 / \u2191")
    if (eff < -0.1) return("\u2014 / \u2193")
    return("\u2014")
  }
  if (eff > 0.2) return("\u2191")
  if (eff < -0.2) return("\u2193")
  "\u2014"
}

# ── Play mode (Score) ──
# Score: lower is better, so negate effects for consistent arrow direction (positive = improvement)
score_p <- c(model = fs_get_p(play_score_anova_result, "model_name"),
             prompt = fs_get_p(play_score_anova_result, "prompt_style"),
             thinking = fs_get_p(play_score_anova_result, "enable_thinking"),
             vot = fs_get_p(play_score_anova_result, "vot_condition"))
score_chi <- c(model = fs_get_chi(play_score_anova_result, "model_name"),
               prompt = fs_get_chi(play_score_anova_result, "prompt_style"),
               thinking = fs_get_chi(play_score_anova_result, "enable_thinking"),
               vot = fs_get_chi(play_score_anova_result, "vot_condition"))
score_dom <- fs_find_dominant(score_p, score_chi)

# Compute score marginals (negate: positive = improvement = lower score)
score_by_model <- play_data |> group_by(model_name) |> summarise(ms = mean(score), .groups = "drop")
score_model_eff <- diff(range(score_by_model$ms))  # always positive (models differ)
score_by_prompt <- play_data |> group_by(prompt_style) |> summarise(ms = mean(score), .groups = "drop")
score_prompt_eff <- fs_safe_diff(score_by_prompt$ms, score_by_prompt$prompt_style,
                                 "baseline", "augmented")  # positive if augmented lowers score
score_by_thinking <- play_data |> group_by(enable_thinking) |> summarise(ms = mean(score), .groups = "drop")
score_think_eff <- fs_safe_diff(score_by_thinking$ms,
                                ifelse(score_by_thinking$enable_thinking, "Enabled", "Disabled"),
                                "Disabled", "Enabled")  # positive if thinking lowers score

# VoT individual effects in score (negate: positive = improvement)
score_by_vot <- play_data |> group_by(vot_condition) |> summarise(ms = mean(score), .groups = "drop")
score_vot_none <- score_by_vot$ms[score_by_vot$vot_condition == "None"]
if (length(score_vot_none) == 0) score_vot_none <- NA_real_

fs_vot_eff_score <- function(pat) {
  if (is.na(score_vot_none)) return(0)
  v <- score_by_vot$ms[grepl(pat, score_by_vot$vot_condition)]
  if (length(v) == 0) 0 else -(v[1] - score_vot_none)  # negate: lower score = positive
}

# Score VoT thresholds scaled to score range (~20-37)
fs_vot_arrow_score <- function(p_overall, eff) {
  if (is.na(p_overall) || p_overall >= 0.10) return("\u2014")
  if (p_overall >= 0.05) {
    if (eff > 0.5) return("\u2014 / \u2191")
    if (eff < -0.5) return("\u2014 / \u2193")
    return("\u2014")
  }
  if (eff > 1.0) return("\u2191")
  if (eff < -1.0) return("\u2193")
  "\u2014"
}

# ── Build table ──
fs_tbl <- tibble(
  Factor = c("Model", "Augmented prompt", "Extended thinking",
             "VoT: Grid State", "VoT: Ray Trace", "VoT: Hypothesis"),
  Predict = c(
    fs_arrow(pred_p["model"], pred_model_eff, fs_is_dom(pred_dom, "model")),
    fs_arrow(pred_p["prompt"], pred_prompt_eff, fs_is_dom(pred_dom, "prompt")),
    fs_arrow(pred_p["thinking"], pred_think_eff, fs_is_dom(pred_dom, "thinking")),
    "\u2014",
    fs_arrow(pred_p["vot"], pred_vot_eff, fs_is_dom(pred_dom, "vot")),
    "\u2014"
  ),
  `Play (Atoms)` = c(
    fs_arrow(play_p["model"], play_model_eff, fs_is_dom(play_dom, "model")),
    fs_arrow(play_p["prompt"], play_prompt_eff, fs_is_dom(play_dom, "prompt")),
    fs_arrow(play_p["thinking"], play_think_eff, fs_is_dom(play_dom, "thinking")),
    fs_vot_arrow(play_p["vot"], fs_vot_eff("Grid")),
    fs_vot_arrow(play_p["vot"], fs_vot_eff("Ray")),
    fs_vot_arrow(play_p["vot"], fs_vot_eff("Hyp"))
  ),
  `Play (Score)` = c(
    fs_arrow(score_p["model"], score_model_eff, fs_is_dom(score_dom, "model")),
    fs_arrow(score_p["prompt"], score_prompt_eff, fs_is_dom(score_dom, "prompt")),
    fs_arrow(score_p["thinking"], score_think_eff, fs_is_dom(score_dom, "thinking")),
    fs_vot_arrow_score(score_p["vot"], fs_vot_eff_score("Grid")),
    fs_vot_arrow_score(score_p["vot"], fs_vot_eff_score("Ray")),
    fs_vot_arrow_score(score_p["vot"], fs_vot_eff_score("Hyp"))
  )
)

# Interpretation across all three columns
fs_interpret <- function(pred, atoms, score) {
  up <- function(x) x %in% c("\u2191", "\u2191\u2191")
  strong <- function(x) x == "\u2191\u2191"
  down <- function(x) x == "\u2193"
  none <- function(x) x == "\u2014"

  pu <- up(pred); au <- up(atoms); su <- up(score)
  sd <- down(score); an <- none(atoms); sn <- none(score)
  pn <- none(pred)

  if (pu && au && su) {
    if (strong(atoms) || strong(score)) "Strong consistent benefit"
    else "Consistent benefit"
  }
  else if (pn && au && su) "Helps play only"
  else if (pu && au && sn) "Helps accuracy, not efficiency"
  else if (pn && au && sn) "Helps atoms only"
  else if (pn && an && sd) "Hurts efficiency only"
  else if (pu && an && sn) "Helps predict only"
  else if (au && sd) "Improves atoms; hurts score"
  else if (pn && an && sn) "Minimal effect"
  else "Mixed effects"
}

fs_tbl$Interpretation <- mapply(fs_interpret, fs_tbl$Predict, fs_tbl$`Play (Atoms)`,
                                fs_tbl$`Play (Score)`, USE.NAMES = FALSE)

gt(fs_tbl) |>
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = c(Predict, `Play (Atoms)`, `Play (Score)`)) |>
  cols_align(align = "left", columns = c(Factor, Interpretation)) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = Factor)
  ) |>
  tab_options(
    table.font.size = px(30),
    column_labels.font.size = px(30),
    column_labels.font.weight = "bold"
  )
```

::: notes
Factor summary derived from the ANOVA results and marginal means. Three outcome columns: Predict (binary accuracy), Play Atoms (0–4 correct), and Play Score (composite penalty, lower is better). The double-arrow indicates the dominant factor — its chi-squared is at least twice the runner-up among significant terms. Single arrows indicate significant effects (p < 0.05). Mixed arrows (— / ↑) indicate marginal significance (0.05 ≤ p < 0.10). Dashes indicate non-significant effects. The Score column reveals divergences from atoms correct: VoT Hypothesis actively hurts score (increases ray use without improving placement), and VoT Ray Trace's atom benefit doesn't survive the composite metric. The key takeaway: you can't prompt your way to diagnostic reasoning. The limitations appear to be in the model's ability to maintain and manipulate internal state, not in the instructions it receives.
:::

## Benchmark Context {visibility="hidden"}

How does Black Box compare to other reasoning benchmarks?

| Benchmark | Task Type | OOD? | Ceiling? | Decomposable? | Process? |
|------------|------------|:----------:|:----------:|:----------:|:----------:|
| ZebraLogic | Constraint satisfaction | Partial | No | No | No |
| ConstraintBench | Constraint satisfaction | Yes | No | No | No |
| BALROG | Game playing | Yes | No | Partial | Yes |
| PuzzlePlex | Puzzle solving | Yes | No | No | No |
| **Black Box** | **Diagnostic reasoning** | **Yes** | **Yes** | **Yes** | **Yes** |

::: fragment
Black Box is unique in providing an **information-theoretic ceiling** and **partial decomposition** into component processes via the two-mode design.
:::

::: notes
How Black Box compares to other reasoning benchmarks. Most benchmarks test constraint satisfaction or puzzle solving but lack key properties. Black Box is the only one that provides an information-theoretic ceiling — we can compute exactly how well a perfect agent would do. And it's the only one that partially decomposes into component processes through the predict/play design. The ceiling is critical because it lets us measure not just whether models succeed or fail, but how far they are from optimal.
:::

## Implications for Deploying LLMs for Clinical and Scientific Reasoning {background-color="#f8f9fa"}

**Thesis**: The frontiers of medicine and science inherently demand first-principles reasoning.

::: fragment
**The verdict** — When forced to reason from first principles on a diagnostic task, LLMs do poorly
:::

::: incremental
1. **Test selection fails** — Models can't design informative experiments. They rarely pick the most informative ray.

2. **Constraint integration fails** — Models don't maintain consistent evidence across reasoning steps. Contradicted hypotheses persist; evidence that should rule out a possibility is ignored.

3. **Scaling doesn't bridge the gap** — Larger models improve modestly but remain far from optimal. This appears to be an architectural limitation, not an instructional one.
:::

::: fragment
Pattern matching handles routine cases. **The frontiers require something LLMs don't yet have.**
:::

::: notes
This slide closes the loop on the thesis from the beginning of the talk. We asked whether LLMs have genuine first-principles reasoning capability or whether pattern matching is all there is. Black Box is designed to answer exactly that question — it's out-of-distribution, there are no training patterns to match, and solving it requires the same abductive inference that drives diagnosis and scientific discovery.

The answer: LLMs fail at the specific components that define first-principles reasoning. First, test selection — models rarely pick the most informative experiment, which means they can't drive an efficient diagnostic workup or design informative scientific experiments. Second, constraint integration — they don't maintain consistent evidence sets across reasoning steps, which means contradicted diagnoses would persist in a clinical differential. Third, scaling provides modest improvement but doesn't close the gap, consistent with Shojaee et al.'s finding that reasoning models hit sharp performance thresholds on problems requiring genuine multi-step reasoning.

The punchline ties back to the thesis: pattern matching may suffice for routine clinical cases and well-characterized scientific problems. But the frontier — novel diseases, atypical presentations, new mechanisms, new therapies — lives in exactly the space where LLMs fail.
:::

## Diagnostic Reasoning: What We Found {.smaller}

| Component                 | What This Study Found |
|---------------------------|-----------------------|
| **Hypothesis generation** | Anchor on early guesses regardless of subsequent evidence |
| **Test selection**        | Rarely pick optimal ray (ranks 5–10 of 32); fire 2–3× more rays than needed |
| **Constraint tracking**   | Contradicted hypotheses persist; ruled-out positions not eliminated |
| **Belief updating**       | New evidence often fails to change the working hypothesis |
| **Multistep reasoning**   | Forward ray tracing ~80% accurate — errors even with atoms visible |
| **Integration**           | Consistent predict→play gap: combining components is harder than any alone |

::: notes
This is the same component table from the beginning of the talk, now populated with what we actually found. Walking through each row: Hypothesis generation — models do propose plausible starting positions, but they anchor on those early guesses even when subsequent evidence contradicts them. Test selection — this is one of the clearest failures. The optimal solver picks the most informative ray; models typically pick rays ranked 5th to 10th and use two to three times as many rays as necessary. Constraint tracking — contradicted hypotheses persist. A ray result that should eliminate a candidate position gets ignored. Belief updating — closely related: new evidence often doesn't change the working hypothesis. Multistep reasoning — even in predict mode, where atoms are visible and the model just needs to trace a ray path, accuracy tops out around 96%. And integration — the consistent gap between predict and play performance across all models shows that combining these components is harder than any component alone. The bottom line: the failures are overwhelmingly in the inferential machinery — test selection, constraint tracking, belief updating — not in spatial reasoning itself.
:::

## Limitations & Future Work

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Limitations

-   Black Box is spatial; not all diagnosis is
-   Fixed action space (32 rays); clinical tests are open-ended
-   Currently only Claude models tested
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Future Directions

-   Identify similar medical domains and test there
-   Test more model families (GPT, Gemini, open-source)
-   Test agentic architectures and harnesses with tool access
-   Fine tune an LLM to Predict, then test
-   Fine tune an LLM to Play, then test
:::
:::::

::: notes
Honest limitations. Black Box is a spatial game, and not all diagnostic reasoning is spatial. The action space is constrained — in real medicine, you choose from thousands of possible tests. And we've only tested Claude models. Future work should test more models, explore multi-agent settings, and — most importantly — test whether Black Box performance predicts performance on actual clinical diagnostic tasks. That transfer analysis would validate the benchmark.
:::
